senses: Someone's house or home.
ety: Abbreviation of domicile, ultimately from Latin domus (“house, home”).
examples: Harry Shapiro was crazy about musicians so we headed straight for his dommy.

senses: A long ornamented skirt or petticoat, tightened with a drawstring and often hung with bells, worn in Rajasthan and other parts of India.
ety: From Hindi घाघरा (ghāghrā), from Sanskrit [Term?].
examples: She's wearing a screeching yellow silk ghagra with a pink chunni.

senses: Small, rigid Japanese playing cards with colorful drawings of flowers and animals, a single deck consisting of 48 cards divided in 12 suits that each represent a month.
ety: From Japanese 花(はな)札(ふだ) (hanafuda), a compound of 花 (hana, “flower”) + 札 (fuda, “card”).
examples: Couldn't we play with hanafuda cards instead? I asked. I had a decent amount of experience with oichokabu or koi koi thanks to playing with my mom's family in the countryside.
Briefly, Sin described the Hanafuda playing cards and how he had adapted them to his own ends.
On a different occasion, he was playing hanafuda in a mountain hut with several Japanese.

senses: An instance or the act of yielding nothing.
ety: Deverbal from strike out.
examples: We've had one strikeout after the other on the Jones account.

senses: A mountain top or rocky element of a ridge that is surrounded by glacial ice but is not covered by ice; a peak protruding from the surface ice sheet.
ety: Borrowed from Greenlandic nunataq.
examples: We made for a slope close to the end of the island or nunatak, where Shackleton must have got up also; it is obviously the only place when you look at it from a commanding rise.
Only a few lichens and mosses colonize the rocky walls of cirques and nunataks.
The peak in whose lee you have chosen to set up your command post is far too regular in shape to be the nunatak you imagine it.

senses: A trench cut in the soil, as when plowed in order to plant a crop.
A deep wrinkle in the skin of the face, especially on the forehead.
ety: From Middle English forow, furgh, from Old English furh, from Proto-West Germanic *furh, from Proto-Germanic *furhs (compare Saterland Frisian Fuurge, Dutch voor, German Furche, Swedish fåra, Norwegian Bokmål fure), from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ- (“to dig”). Compare Welsh rhych (“furrow”), Latin porca (“ridge, balk”), Lithuanian prapar̃šas (“ditch”), Sanskrit पर्शान (párśāna, “chasm”).
examples: Don't walk across that deep furrow in the field.

The family feeling was intensified as we stopped to speak to mothers in the cottage gardens, or waved to distant tractors turning over chocolate-brown furrows and driven by 'my dad' or 'my Uncle Bob'.
When she was tired, a deep furrow appeared on her forehead.

senses: Full of rapture.
ety: From rapture + -ous.
examples: Díaz told a rapturous crowd of 5,000 who turned out in Madrid on Sunday for the launch: “I want to be Spain’s first female president because women’s time has come, and women want to be the ones who make history.”
Both players were given rapturous rounds of applause as they collected their trophies after the second longest major final in history.

senses: To hang downward; to sag.
To slowly become limp; to bend gradually.
To lose all energy, enthusiasm or happiness; to flag.
To allow to droop or sink.
To proceed downward, or toward a close; to decline.
ety: Inherited from Middle English droupen, from Old Norse drúpa (“to droop”), from Proto-Germanic *drūpaną, *drupōną (“to hang down, drip, drop”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewb- (“to drip, drop”). Doublet of drip and drop.
examples: On the brown harvest tree / Droops the red cherry.
Good things of day begin to droop and drowse; / While night’s black agents to their preys do rouse.
Others who conscientiously attended the Technical College at night often drooped over their desks in a doze, and one does not wonder at it.

senses: A lozenge; a cough drop.
ety: Medical English got troche and trochiscus from late Latin trochiscus; from Ancient Greek τρόχισκος (trókhiskos, “a small ball”), ultimately from Ancient Greek τροχός (trokhós, “wheel”).
examples: The Germ. Pharm. states that the troches (pastilles) are to be made by compression or by massing with a suitable excipient, and forming into troches.
The troches are weighed and the average weight per troche for that base is calculated.

senses: To exude or yield.
ety: First directly attested in 1728; attested as the past-participial adjective secreted in 1707: from Latin sēcrētus, perfect passive participle of sēcernō (“to separate”); reinforced by back-formation from secretion; compare secern; cognate with French sécréter and the Spanish secretar.
examples: If you won’t believe my great new doctrine (which, by the bye, is as old as the Greeks), that souls secrete their bodies, as snails do shells, you will remain in outer darkness.

senses: The track cut out by a scythe in mowing.
A broad sweep or expanse, such as of land or of people.
ety: From Middle English swath, swathe, from Old English swæþ, swaþu (“track; trace; footstep”), from Proto-Germanic *swaþō (“a wind-swept place; open field”), of unknown further origin. Has been derived from a Proto-Indo-European *swey- (“to bend, turn, swing”), and compared with Ancient Greek σιμός (simós, “snub-nosed”) and Welsh chwil (“reeling, staggering”), though this is uncertain, as well as the Greek comparandum being unlikely. Cognate with Dutch zwade, zwad (“swath; windrow”), German Schwade (“swath; windrow”), Icelandic svæði (“area; zone; sector; region”). other etymological information
examples: A large swath of the population is opposed to this government policy.
Five days after Hurricane Katrina, large swaths of New Orleans are still submerged in water.
It is undeniable that Malcolm was a beacon of huge strength in his lifetime. He could connect with swaths of people when others could not.

senses: A star used as a navigation reference, particularly a pole star such as Polaris.
A guiding tenet or principle.
ety: From Middle English lode (“journey, course”) + star, where lode is an archaic noun from the verb lithe (“to go, journey”), related to lead. Other Middle English spellings include: 14th century loode sterre, lood-sterre, lade-sterne; and 15th century lode sterre. Cognate with Old Norse leiðarstjarna, Dutch leidster, German Leitstern, Danish ledestjerne, Swedish ledstjärna.
examples: He was no wavering mariner; he had taken his course from a single lodestar, by which he had steered from the first day he had seen it in his heavens — the lodestar that had shone for him and would always shine.
We need a new lodestar, a new map of the world that once again includes a distant, uncharted continent—“Utopia.”

With export controls still restricting the sale of the most advanced chips to China and its university students increasingly unwelcome in the U.S., technological self-sufficiency has become Beijing’s lodestar.

senses: A section of a European newspaper typically dedicated to arts, culture, criticism, and light literature.
An article published in such a section.
ety: Borrowed from French feuilleton.
examples: Now and then, when luck had favoured me, I had managed to get five shillings for a feuilleton from some newspaper or other.

The feuilleton, like the other serious, trivial, and merely curious stories on the newspaper page, served up an excess of details. For the most part, the feuilleton writer observed, rather than explained.

senses: A magician; (derogatory) a conjurer or sorcerer, especially one who is a charlatan or trickster.
ety: From Latin magus, from Ancient Greek μάγος (mágos, “magician”), from Μάγος (Mágos, “Magian”), of an indeterminate Old Iranian origin (see Μάγος for details). Doublet of mage.
examples: It’s from our venerable maguses Gominik Halvor and his son. They’ve cast the runes for our enterprise.

senses: The young of a swan.
ety: From Middle English cignet, signet, from Anglo-Norman cignet, diminutive of Old French cigne (“swan”), from Latin cygnus, cycnus (“swan”), from Ancient Greek κύκνος (kúknos, “swan”).
examples: I am the cygnet to this pale faint swan, Who chants a doleful hymn to his own death, And from the organ-pipe of frailty sings His soul and body to their lasting rest.

senses: Characterized by open fields and an agricultural economy; agricultural.
ety: From field + -en (“pertaining to, of the nature of”).
examples: Religious ignorance was probably particularly common in the heath and forest areas, where society was less rigid and disciplined than in the stable, nucleated villages of the fielden communities.
The reader should remember that husbandmen in fielden parishes formed a majority of the rural population.

senses: Marijuana, the inflorescence of the Cannabis sativa plant, smoked or ingested for euphoric effect.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi गांजा (gāñjā), ultimately from Sanskrit गञ्जा (gañjā, “hemp”). First use appears c. 1800.
examples: Whilst a ganja-eater was catching fish on the bank of a river, a man from another country came and asked which was the road and what was his name; he replied that his name was "eater of six maunds of ganja."
In Bengal the natives talk of the ganja-bearing plant as the male and the weaker pollen-bearing plant as the female.
It must be the ganja, it's the marijuana / That's creeping up on me, why I'm so high

senses: A traditional Māori pit oven, in which (suitably wrapped) raw food is lain on a base of heated stones.
Food cooked in this way.
ety: Borrowed from Māori hāngī.
examples: The ovens were used to cook food in identical fashion to the Maori hangi and the Papuan stone ovens.
He glanced at the formal setting in front of him, wishing he could be at a marae eating hangi right now.

senses: A tailed pepper plant (Piper cubeba), an Indonesian plant cultivated for its berries and essential oil.
One of the berries of this plant, used as a condiment.
ety: From Middle English quibibe, from Old French quibibe, cubebe, from Arabic كُبَابَة (kubāba). The current form is remodelled after modern French cubèbe.
examples: Chestnuts, soaked in muscadel, then boiled, along with satyrion, pistachio nuts, pine kernels, cubebs, cinnamon, rocket seed and sugar. Compounded together, these ingredient form a stimulating electuary.

senses: Containing sulfur.
ety: From Latin sulphurōsus. By surface analysis, sulfur + -ous.
examples: The miners slowly walked up the steep crater walls, stopping frequently while clouds of sulfurous gas blanketed the crater in the background.

senses: A spicy Ghanaian sauce made with seafood, tomatoes, garlic, peppers, and spices.
ety: From Ga shito (“pepper”).
examples: The quantity of the ground tomato, pepper, salt and onion is mixed with the smashed smoked fish and boiled in oil for about two hours and bottled. The bottled shito is found on the markets in Ghana and abroad.

senses: Having large breasts; busty.
ety: From breast + -y.
examples: Blue-eyed, fair-haired and rosy-cheeked, she was not, it is true, either lithe or lath-like, but then had not Tommo once expressed a preference for breasty girls?

senses: To loiter about casually or idly, to hang around unproductively, to laze around or relax.
ety: Borrowed from Malay lepak.
examples: We do things together and we lepak together quite a bit (hey, this is the solution to the lepak problem: the family that lepaks together stays together).
The study's operational definition was that "a teenager lepaks if he gathers and remains in a public place without any special purpose other than chattering or laughing."

senses: A person or thing that ejaculates.
A device that stimulates the sex organs of a male animal with electric impulses in order to extract semen from an animal.
ety: From ejaculate + -or.
examples: Some experts have described the premature ejaculator as a man who cannot control his ejaculation for at least thirty seconds after penetration. Others have suggested one minute.

senses: To make beautiful; to increase the beauty of.
ety: From Middle English beutifien, from Old French beaute (“beauty”), from Latin bellus (“beautiful, fine”), + -ify, from Latin facio (“make”).
examples: Officials are taking these old palm trees down in several parks and public spaces as they try to beautify the city, and prevent rotting tree trunks from falling on people.

senses: A white grape variety; used as table grapes and for making raisins and sweet wine.
The muscatel wine made from these grapes.
The vine bearing this fruit.
ety: Borrowed from French muscat.
examples: Among Turks, pills consisting of hemp buds, muscat nuts, saffron, and honey were a popular aphrodisiac.

senses: In the capacity of a matron; serving as a housekeeper or head nurse.
Exuding the authority, wisdom, power, and intelligence of an experienced woman.
Having the appearance of a mature woman, often of larger physical stature and somewhat unkempt or dowdy.
ety: From matron + -ly.
examples: The door opened, but it was to admit a middle-aged matronly lady with good-humour and domestic capability proclaimed by every detail of her smiling face and easy manner.

senses: Causing sorrow, distress or regret; deplorable, pitiful or distressing.
ety: From Middle English lamentable, from Middle French lamentable, from Latin lāmentābilis (“full of sorrow, mournful; deplorable”), from lāmentor (“lament”), from lāmenta (“wailing, weeping”). By surface analysis, lament + -able.
examples: Moreover, in view of the lamentable present indecision of the Government in regard to electrification, the large-scale building of diesel power may prove to have been a farseeing move after all.

senses: A poisonous cardiac glycoside, g-strophanthin, found in the seeds of certain lianas.
ety: From ouaba(io) + -in, after French ouabain, ultimately from Somali waabaayo, meaning "arrow poison".
examples: In moderate dosage ouabain is used today to treat emergency heart failure; in excessive doses it makes the heart go crazy, pumping wildly until it collapses.

senses: An imaginary flower that does not wither.
The characteristic purplish-red colour of the flowers or leaves of these plants.
The seed of these plants, used as a cereal.
ety: Borrowed from French amarante, or directly from its etymon Latin amarantus (the word ending influenced by plant names derived from Ancient Greek ἄνθος (ánthos, “a bloom, blossom, flower”)), from Ancient Greek ἀμάραντος (amárantos, “eternal, undying, unfading, unwilting; amaranth; everlasting flower”) (modern Greek αμάραντος (amárantos)), from ᾰ̓- (ă-, the alpha privativum, a prefix forming words having a sense opposite to the word or stem to which it is attached) + μαραίνω (maraínō, “to shrivel, wither”) + -τος (-tos, suffix forming adjectives).
examples: Or, propt on beds of amaranth and moly, / How sweet (while warm airs lull us, blowing lowly,)
The Amaranth’s snowy blossoms, stormwoven, / Shed their soft lustre, o’er thy forehead fair! / By seraph hands the fadeless wreath was woven, / And twined amid thy sunny locks of hair.

senses: A public telephone that requires prepayment to operate, generally via the insertion of coins or a credit card.
ety: From pay + phone.
examples: I only had ten cents in my pocket, so I couldn't use the payphone to call a cab.
You called me from a payphone / They still got payphones / It costs a dollar a minute / To tell me you're getting sober

senses: A small towel, hand or face wipe, either dry or more commonly impregnated with water or a cleansing fluid.
ety: From towel + -ette.
examples: The folded moist towelette was smaller than my palm, but when unfolded at least cleaned my hands.

senses: Not mannerly (“polite; having good manners”).
ety: From Middle English unmanerli (“of a person: disorderly, unruly; of conduct: inappropriate, improper”), from un- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + manerli, manerly (“well-mannered; modest; customary; moral”). Manerli is derived from maner (“kind, sort; form, nature; circumstances; method, manner; outward behaviour, manners; morals; custom, usage; cause, reason”) (from Anglo-Norman, Old French manere (“fashion, manner, way”), from Latin manuārius (“of or pertaining to the hand”), from manus (“hand”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”)) + -li (suffix forming adjectives). The Engl
examples: Halloa! whew! there goes my tarpaulin overboard; Lord, Lord, that the winds that come from heaven should be so unmannerly! This is a nasty night, lad.
So you will allow me to be insulted by an unmannerly bastard in your home?

senses: The science of sending, receiving and storing information by means of telecommunication devices.
The use of Global Positioning System technology integrated with computers and mobile communications technology.
ety: Calque of French télématique.
examples: Telematics is often used in road vehicles.

senses: To increase the humidity in the air.
ety: From humid + -ify.
examples: The air-handling equipment humidifies, dehumidifies, and distributes the correct amount of fresh air into every zone and eliminates all smoke, dust, and odors, with electric precipitrons.

senses: Something which links two things of greater significance than itself.
An enclosed walkway or passage that connects two buildings.
Someone who belongs to a marginalized subgroup, and can therefore described by a hyphenated term, such as "German-American", "female-academic", etc.
ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin hyphen, from Ancient Greek ῠ̔φέν (hŭphén, “in one, as a single word”), univerbation of ῠ̔φ’ ἕν (hŭph’ hén, “under one”), from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, “under”) + ἕν (hén, “one”), neuter of εἷς (heîs, “one”).
examples: Cunliffe and Karunanayake (2013) developed Fine's notion to introduce potential hyphen spaces that are deeply implicated and reciprocally influential in relationships between researchers and the researched.
The hyphens were added, joining the structures into one building, which now measures just over two hundred feet long.
Construction details for the hyphens, or "connecting wings" as they were called by the contractors, were included in the contractors' specifications, as follows:

senses: Something which ends another thing.
ety: From Middle English endere, ender; equivalent to end (verb) + -er (agent noun suffix).
examples: The papal paragraph quoted at the outset of this essay is a starting point for some future intervention, not an argument ender that anyone in Silicon Valley is likely to accept.

senses: A man who plows land with a plow.
ety: From Middle English plowman, ploghmon, plouȝman, equivalent to plow + man. Compare Middle Dutch ploechman.
examples: A cereal breeder's farmhands must be good plowmen.

senses: Capable of being finely or idly adjusted with the fingers.
Having an elaborately twisted form.
In music, having a rapid series of musical notes.
ety: From twiddle + -y.
examples: Radio – with its buttons and twiddly knobs and white noise in between – is on the tip of a huge wave of change, courtesy of the Internet.
It was her nose was the worst. It seemed to have been twisted into a hook with a twiddly bit at the top.
The bugle called, a twiddly bit and then one long note.

senses: The doctrine that faith is the basis of all knowledge.
ety: From French fidéisme, from Latin fidēs + -isme. By surface analysis, Latin fide- + -ism.
examples: We were warned at Cambridge, your grace, of the dangers of what is termed fideism.
